name: Vedic chant
lineage: Vedic chant — the canonical three-thousand-year-continuous Sanskrit recitation tradition for the four Vedas (Rgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda) preserved through the gurukula master-disciple oral-transmission lineage; defined by the three-tone udatta-anudatta-svarita pitch-accent system (udatta the raised pitch, anudatta the lower pitch, svarita the falling-pitch tone) inherited from Proto-Indo-European prosody, with the additional Sāmaveda musical-melodic elaboration (the Sāman chant tradition that uses seven svaras and is considered the source of later Indian classical raga); transmission preserved through the canonical paṭha (recitation-style) variants — Saṃhitā (continuous), Padapāṭha (word-by-word), Krama-pāṭha (interlocking pairs), Jaṭā-pāṭha (woven pattern), and Ghana-pāṭha (dense pattern) — each designed to lock the text against transmission error; the Nambudiri Brahmin community of Kerala preserves the most archaic Sāmavedic chanting layer, with parallel Tamil-Brahmin, Maharashtrian, and Kashi (Banaras) regional preservation lineages
